page8_img_1.png.title: Graph rewiring example: swapping minor contribution edges
page8_img_1.png.description: Two-panel schematic showing how contribution edges are rewired while preserving node degrees. Panel (a) “before” depicts two developer nodes (Amy, Bob) each connected by a labeled “minor” edge to distinct binary nodes (C and D). Panel (b) “after” shows the same developers and binaries but with the minor edges crossed (Amy→D, Bob→C), illustrating an edge-swap that keeps each developer’s and binary’s number of minor contributions constant while randomizing which components they touch; the paper uses this rewiring repeatedly to generate randomized contribution graphs for statistical tests of the major-minor-dependency phenomenon.

page4_img_1.png.title: Developer ownership distributions for A.dll and B.dll
page4_img_1.png.description: Two side-by-side plots showing the percentage of commits by developers (ordered decreasing) for two Windows binaries. The y-axis is percent of commits (0–60%), the x-axis indexes developers sorted by contribution; a red horizontal line marks the 5% threshold that separates major (blue diamonds) from minor (red circles) contributors. (a) A.dll is concentrated: the top developer accounts for ~49% of commits, there are four major contributors and four minor contributors. (b) B.dll is diffuse: the top developer accounts for ~22% of commits, there are still four major contributors but 74 minor contributors — a profile the paper links to much higher pre‑ and post‑release failure counts (B.dll had ~8× more pre‑release and ~2× more post‑release failures than A.dll) and greater size/churn.

page7_img_1.png.title: Major–Minor–Dependency example: owner edits a dependent binary
page7_img_1.png.description: The schematic shows two binaries as yellow ovals — Foo.exe (top) and Bar.dll (bottom) — linked by a blue arrow labeled “Dependency” from Foo.exe to Bar.dll. A green arrow labeled “Major Contributor” points from a developer (off to the left) to Foo.exe, while a red arrow labeled “Minor Contributor” points from the same developer to Bar.dll, illustrating a developer who is an owner of one component but only a minor contributor to a component it depends on. The paper uses this Major–Minor–Dependency pattern to explain a common maintenance behavior and to motivate the statistical analysis (they found this relationship for 52% of binaries in Vista versus about 24% in randomized graphs).

page5_img_1.png.title: Spearman correlations of ownership and code metrics with pre/post-release failures
page5_img_1.png.description: This table reports Spearman correlation coefficients between ownership metrics (Total, Minor, Major, Ownership) and classic code metrics (Size, Churn, Complexity) versus pre- and post-release failures for Windows Vista and Windows 7. Minor and Total show the strongest positive correlations with pre-release failures (Vista: Total 0.84, Minor 0.86; Windows 7: Total 0.92, Minor 0.93), while Ownership (the top owner’s proportion) is negatively correlated with pre-release failures (Vista −0.49, Windows 7 −0.29), consistent with higher single-owner share relating to fewer faults. Major contributor counts have small or mixed effects (Vista ~0.26, Windows 7 −0.40), and the classic metrics also correlate positively with pre-release failures (Size/Churn/Complexity ≈0.70). Correlations with post-release failures are generally weaker—particularly for Windows 7 (e.g., Ownership ≈ −0.02)—and, per the paper, all reported correlations are statistically significant except Ownership vs. Windows 7 post-release failures.

page6_img_table_1.png.title: Variance explained in failures by adding ownership metrics (Vista & Windows 7)
page6_img_table_1.png.description: The table reports the percent of variance explained (adjusted R²) for models predicting pre- and post-release failures in Windows Vista and Windows 7 as ownership-related variables are added. The Base model (code metrics only) explains 26% (pre) and 29% (post) for Vista and 24% (pre) and 18% (post) for Windows 7. Adding Total contributors increases explained variance (Vista pre: 40% (+14%), post: 35% (+6%); Win7 pre: 68% (+35%), post: 21% (+3%)). Adding Minor contributors yields the largest gains (Vista pre: 46% (+20%), post: 41% (+12%); Win7 pre: 70% (+46%), post: 21% (+3%)). Subsequent additions of Major and Ownership give only small incremental improvements (final models: Vista up to 50% pre / 44% post; Windows 7 up to 72% pre / 22% post). Asterisks in the table indicate cases where the added variable produced a statistically significant improvement.

page10_img_1.png.title: Prediction performance by contribution type for Vista and Windows 7
page10_img_1.png.description: The table gives precision, recall and F-score (percent) for defect predictors trained on contribution networks built from all edges, only minor-contributor edges, or only major-contributor edges, evaluated separately for pre-release and post-release failures in Windows Vista and Windows 7. For pre-release defects both Vista and Windows 7 show high performance for models using all edges (precision ≈89–90%, recall ≈91–92%, F-score ≈90–91%) and models using only minor edges perform nearly as well (precision 87–88%, recall 93%, F-score 89–90%), while major-only models are modestly worse. For post-release Vista the minor-only model actually outperforms the all-edges model (precision 84% vs 75%, recall 88% vs 82%, F-score 86% vs 78%), whereas the major-only model drops sharply (precision 44%, recall 58%, F-score 50%). For Windows 7 post-release all variants have very low precision (8–12%) and low F-scores (14–21%) with minor-only achieving higher recall (75%) but many false positives, illustrating that minor-contributor edges supply most of the useful predictive signal—removing them greatly reduces precision and F-score, especially for post-release prediction.

page3_img_1.png.title: Commit share per developer for abocomp.dll (ownership, major/minor)
page3_img_1.png.description: A ranked dot-plot of the percent of commits to abocomp.dll by 17 developers (x-axis = developer rank, y-axis = percent of commits). The top contributor is highlighted and labeled as making 41.3% of commits (379 of 918); five blue diamonds above the red 5% horizontal line are the major contributors (>=5%), and twelve red circles below that line are minor contributors (<5%). The plot shows a steep drop after the top one or two developers, illustrating one dominant owner and many low-share contributors—matching the paper’s reported metrics: Minor=12, Major=5, Total=17, Ownership=0.41, which the authors use to discuss ownership’s relationship with failures.

page9_img_1.png.title: Developer–binary contribution network (major vs. minor edges)
page9_img_1.png.description: A small bipartite contribution graph where circles are developers (Bob, Ram, Fu, Sara, Amy) and squares are binaries (A, B, C, D); solid lines indicate major-contributor relationships (≥5% of commits) and dashed lines indicate minor-contributor relationships (<5%). For example, Ram is shown as a major contributor to B (solid) and a minor contributor to A (dashed); Fu is a major contributor to B and C but a minor contributor to D; Sara is major on A and C; Amy majors on C and D; Bob appears only as a minor contributor to B. The figure illustrates the common pattern studied in the paper: developers who “own” one binary often make minor changes to related binaries, creating short connecting paths via dashed edges that the authors show carry much of the defect-prediction signal and that, if removed, substantially alter network connectivity and predictive power.
